proposed_edges.relationship: Stoler identifies Said’s Orientalism as a formative resource for thinking about colonial governance and the continuing politics of knowledge.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own 2015 interview, first answer, recalls reading Orientalism while writing her dissertation in Paris in 1978 and says Said and Foucault have differently informed thirty years of work. Her following answers insist that Said’s political project should not be reduced to literary criticism or separated from The Question of Palestine. This records her retrospective interpretation; neither Said book nor Stoler’s complete monographs is newly read.

proposed_edges.relationship: Stoler credits Foucault’s analysis of subordination and his ethics of discomfort as continuing resources for her research while retaining her criticisms of his limits.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own 2015 interview explicitly recalls reading Volonté du savoir alongside Orientalism during dissertation work and says both informed her subsequent work. Answers on Marx and discomfort explain micro-sites of subsumption and vigilance toward ready-made categories. Her stated criticisms of Foucault remain, including existing edge_386. The interview’s parenthetical 1980 English manifestation is not treated as the date of the recalled 1978 reading; exact language or copy is not established. No cited original newly read.

proposed_edges.relationship: Stoler says Marx continues to inform her understanding of exploitation and subordination rather than having been displaced by Foucault.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own 2015 answer explicitly rejects a simple turn from Marx to Foucault, distinguishing Marx’s subsumption from Foucault’s leverage on its micro-sites. She gives feminism equal importance and relates these resources to plantation labor, gender and family arrangements. This bounded retrospective debt names no particular Marx title and does not subsume her work under a single school.

proposed_edges.relationship: Stoler uses Wittgenstein’s rough ground as a resource for investigating concept formation and subject formation in their messy settings.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own 2015 answer on fieldwork in philosophy invokes rough ground to reject remaining in transcendental abstraction and to ask how concepts and subjects form. It is a specific conceptual use, not proof of general discipleship, a direct quotation checked in a Wittgenstein original, or a claim about the whole of her method. The interview’s adjacent “Austen” attribution remains unresolved and is not silently corrected.

proposed_edges.relationship: Stoler criticizes the silence around race in Bourdieu’s account of French bourgeois and middle-class distinction while acknowledging his engaged intellectual practice.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own 2015 fieldwork-in-philosophy answer says Bourdieu did not go far enough and specifies a silent corridor around race in the making of Distinction. This is her particular criticism, alongside acknowledgment that he was an engaged intellectual, rather than a dismissal of all his work. Neither Distinction nor an original reply is newly read; no reciprocal answer is claimed.

proposed_edges.relationship: Stoler adapts de Certeau’s displaced history to examine contrary and disqualified narratives within colonial archives.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own 2007 article opening and note 7 explicitly take up displaced history but qualify the borrowing: Stoler’s use is closer to Foucault’s relation between erudite and disqualified knowledge than to de Certeau’s own definition. She therefore does not simply reproduce his concept. Note 7 identifies Heterologies (1986), “The Theater of the Quiproquo: Alexandre Dumas,” 151, and the Foucault text in the jointly edited Dirks–Eley–Ortner reader. That editorial credit is not a separate personal debt. Cited originals and the complete 2009 book remain unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Stoler uses Ricœur’s account of Aristotle’s distinction between history and poetry to frame her inquiry into colonial imaginaries that move between actual and possible events.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own 2007 paragraph on developing historical negatives invokes Ricœur’s parse of historians’ things that have been and poets’ things that might be, then explains that her ethnographic history moves between fictive, futuristic and concrete. Note 8 cites Time and Narrative, volume 1, Chicago 1984, especially 40–41. The distinction is a resource she works across, not a rule she simply endorses. Neither Ricœur nor Aristotle original newly read; no complete Stoler monograph reading.

proposed_edges.relationship: Stoler explicitly takes Farge’s warning against easy archival familiarity as a resource for reading the fixed formats and apparent obviousness of colonial records.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own 2007 “Archival Conventions” opens with Farge’s warning and says she takes it to heart before specifying the clichéd formats and partial overviews of Netherlands Indies administrative writing. Notes 5 and 10 identify Le goût de l’archive (Paris 1989) and 90. Note 5 separately credits Farge’s material sensations and Steedman’s longings to animate archival relics; their contributions are not conflated. Farge’s original and Stoler’s complete monograph remain unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Ottevaere compares Stoler and Joan Scott as historians who question inherited categories rather than taking them as stable starting points.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Ottevaere’s complete 2004 review, paragraph after discussion of chapters 4 and 5, explicitly compares the careful evaluation of historically designated categories and caution about assumed colonial divisions. This is the named reviewer’s methodological comparison, not direct transmission, personal collaboration or Stoler’s own declaration of a Scott debt. It makes explicit the personal comparison already mentioned within group contribution edge_1218 without replacing that broader gender-history route. Neither original author’s complete monograph newly read.

proposed_edges.relationship: Anderson locates his account of nationalism within a materialist historical formation while seeking to address problems that Marxist traditions had left unresolved.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own 2003 first answer recounts reading nineteenth- and twentieth-century Marxist classics, especially Marx and Lenin, in the antiwar period; later paragraphs describe a materialist history and the problem nationalism posed for mainstream Marxism. His third answer insists on the capitalist commodity character of books while distinguishing their imaginative consumption. Marx is one named resource within this formation, not its sole origin, an endorsement of all Marxist theory, or a newly read original. The Marxist social-history group route 229 remains distinct.

proposed_edges.relationship: Anderson explicitly credits Walter Benjamin with a decisive intellectual impact and uses homogeneous, empty time when explaining the simultaneous connections studied in Under Three Flags.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own complete 2016 retrospective identifies reading New Left Review from 1974 as the encounter with Benjamin that decisively affected him; later discussion of Under Three Flags uses homogeneous, empty time to connect late nineteenth-century political and literary developments across countries. This combines explicit formation with a particular resource rather than inferring influence from a name alone. James Siegel, Auerbach, Victor Turner and the wider NLR circle retain their distinct credits; no Benjamin original or complete monograph newly read. Posthumous 2016 publication is distinct from the narrated 1970s formation and 2005 book.

proposed_edges.relationship: Anderson identifies Geertz’s defense of Javanese rationality as a resource in developing his comparative inquiry into political power.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own 2016 retrospective recalls the 1965–66 Encounter dispute with Herbert Lüthy and sides with Geertz’s “Are the Javanese Mad?” while explaining that his own question moved toward a systematic historical study of rationality. The account gives chance stimuli and substantive help distinct roles: Allan Bloom’s overheard remark, Moertono’s thesis and conversations, and Geertz’s defense are not collapsed into one source. The adjacent claim about ancient Greek power is challenged in Colin Wells’s displayed letter; it is not certified here. Neither Encounter original nor the complete 1972 essay newly read.

proposed_edges.relationship: Anderson criticizes Gellner’s functional linkage of nationalism to industrialism for underexplaining early American nationalisms, language and emotional attachment.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own 2003 third answer explicitly calls the criticism mild and specifies early nationalism in the Americas before industrialism, the emotional force of national belonging and the imaginative power of writing. This is Anderson’s characterized disagreement, not a new independent adjudication of Gellner’s whole theory. His first answer says he read the earlier nationalism piece in Thought and Change rather than the 1983 Nations and Nationalism while preparing Imagined Communities; no unverified original passage locator is invented. A separate positive linguistic resource is retained.

proposed_edges.relationship: Anderson credits Gellner’s explanation of aristocratic linguistic distinction when discussing hierarchies within Europe.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own 2003 answer to the colonial/peripheral Russia comparison points to French-speaking Amsterdam elites and German-speaking Prague elites, then explicitly credits Gellner for explaining aristocracies’ linguistic distinction from surrounding populations. It is a bounded explanatory resource within an argument against a single undifferentiated West, alongside disagreement about nationalism’s functional explanation. The witness does not identify which Gellner title supports this particular point; no title, full-theory endorsement or original reading is inferred.

proposed_edges.relationship: Ginzburg questions Anderson’s metaphor of studying empires as extinct dinosaurs, suggesting that imperial forms will remain present while expressing admiration for Anderson’s work.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own original 2006 interview’s final exchange explicitly names and admires Anderson, then disputes the dinosaur analogy and predicts that such dinosaurs will remain around. This is a narrow disagreement about imperial persistence, not a rejection of Imagined Communities or all nationalism theory. Anderson’s actual 2003 final answer distinguishes weakening nation-states from persistent nationalism, calls for careful comparative study of different empires, and frames the dinosaur remark within that discussion. Ginzburg’s prediction retains his own uncertainty; neither speaker’s historical forecast is certified as fact.

proposed_edges.relationship: Johnson invokes Chakrabarty’s criticism of universal historical subjects to qualify Genovese’s resistance-to-revolution teleology.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own On Agency, 117 and123/note11, identifies the problem of translating African forms of resistance into a Western Marxist trajectory whose endpoint is a liberal individual and rights language. His note explicitly directs readers to Provincializing Europe as a pointed critique of arguments of this kind. This is a bounded argumentative resource, not proof that Chakrabarty originated every objection or a new reading of his book. Existing Genovese critique1609 remains consolidated and exact.

proposed_edges.relationship: Johnson draws on Hall’s discussion of the historical subject when questioning an undifferentiated agent of enslaved resistance.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own On Agency, 117–118 and123/note12, asks how differently situated subjects—mother, Christian, Igbo or Blacks—understood their actions, rather than assuming a universal individual slave. The note specifically supplies Hall’s The Toad in the Garden and, from a different perspective, Joan Scott’s The Evidence of Experience. Both resources are retained as distinct contributions; no shared doctrine, direct personal exchange or new original essay reading is claimed.

proposed_edges.relationship: Johnson invokes Joan Scott’s Evidence of Experience as a resource for questioning the assumed subject of histories of enslaved agency.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own On Agency, 118 and123/note12, links the question of who acted and in what historical idiom to Scott’s essay, expressly distinguished from Stuart Hall’s perspective in the same note. The resource helps interrogate an unqualified individual slave as historical subject; it does not deny that enslaved people acted, attribute every part of Johnson’s analysis to Scott or establish a personal meeting. Scott’s original essay remains unread in this continuation.

proposed_edges.relationship: Johnson explicitly uses Benjamin’s Arcades Project as a framework for studying how the past becomes active in present struggles over memory.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own On Agency,119 and123/note16, proposes reversing a simple past-to-present cultural transmission model by examining how historically situated people select and enforce elements of a shared past. He identifies Benjamin’s Arcades Project, especially456–488 in the1999 translation, and Harry Harootunian’s History’s Disquiet as the theoretical framework. Joint credit remains explicit, alongside differential power by gender, age and origin. Neither cited original nor translation is newly read; no wholesale Benjamin lineage inferred.

proposed_edges.relationship: Johnson uses Du Bois’s accounts of slavery, empire and differentiated labor as resources for a history of racial capitalism.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own To Remake the World,2017, develops sustained readings of The Souls of White Folk, Black Reconstruction and The World and Africa. He treats plantation, counting house and factory as differentiated but interconnected components, retaining racial and geographical distinctions rather than asserting that all white workers benefited equally. Cedric Robinson’s Black Marxism supplies an explicitly acknowledged interpretive route, not hidden sole Du Bois credit. This is Johnson’s specific analytical use in the essay, not proof of the origins of his1999 or2013books or a fresh reading of the cited originals.

proposed_edges.relationship: Johnson uses Eric Williams’s account of British emancipation and slave-grown cotton to connect industrial capitalism with continuing Atlantic slavery.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own To Remake the World,2017, explicitly invokes Capitalism and Slavery1944 for the shift from colonial sugar interests to manufacturing and cotton, arguing that British emancipation did not remove slavery from British economic relations. This is his attributed use of Williams as part of an argument against separating Manchester from Mississippi; the original1944book and underlying trade statistics are not freshly audited. It is not agreement with every Williams thesis or a claim about a teacher or personal encounter.

proposed_edges.relationship: Johnson challenges Davis’s animalization explanation of slavery and emancipation, arguing that it conflates ideological doctrine with enslaved experience.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own Brute Ideology2014:130–132 distinguishes what Davis actually claims from a literal assertion that enslaved people were animals, then questions the mass-psychological explanatory frame. Johnson uses Barbara Fields’s doctrine/ideology distinction and a close reading of black abolitionists’ word brute to contest Davis’s interpretation. He explicitly thanks Davis for defining the field, acknowledges the importance of affective harm and retains the achievement of abolition. His is a specific, qualified review judgment, not an independent audit of Davis’s full trilogy, black abolitionist originals or a denial of violence.

proposed_edges.relationship: Valverde explicitly places her work in Foucault’s tradition of developing theoretical tools through concrete historical research.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own What Counts as Theory, Today? (2016), 174 and178, expressly identifies her Foucauldian working tradition and uses power/knowledge to explain how jurisdiction assigns different forms of governance. Her adoption of Bakhtin is explicitly an additional resource rather than abandonment of Foucault, while she rejects automatic eclecticism. This is a qualified intellectual debt stated in2016, not a first-publication date for her1991method or a claim that all her work derives from one thinker. Existing group route858 retains its broader moral-regulation context; original Foucault works are not newly read.

proposed_edges.relationship: Valverde uses Derrida’s Spectres of Marx to challenge the opposition between theoretical sophistication and politically engaged labour history.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own Deconstructive Marxism (1995),332–338, calls the book a resource for rethinking the theory/politics and ideal/material oppositions, while preserving Marx’s emancipatory project and the importance of historical inheritance. Her339–340 discussion explicitly stops short of Derrida’s undeconstructible justice and expresses reservations about its mystical context. The specific positive resource coexists with her earlier critique of Scott967; it is not a blanket endorsement, proof of personal contact or a new reading of Derrida’s original or Peggy Kamuf’s1994translation. Lorna Weir’s explicitly acknowledged help with deconstruction remains separate.
